title_en: Joseph Moore: The Investments That Matter Most May Not Be in Your Portfolio
title_zh: Joseph Moore：最值得投资的东西，也许不在你的组合里
subtitle_zh: 历史学家Joseph Moore纵览美国三百年理财建议，拆解婚姻、职业与集中度这些真正决定财富的变量。
description: Joseph Moore: The Investments That Matter Most May Not Be in Your Portfolio

turns.en: Please stay tuned for important disclosure information at the conclusion of this episode. Hi, and welcome to the Long View. I'm Amy Arnott, portfolio strategist for Morningstar.
turns.zh: 节目结尾有重要的披露信息，敬请期待。大家好，欢迎收听The Long View。我是Amy Arnott，Morningstar的组合策略师。

turns.en: And I'm Christine Benz, director of personal finance and retirement planning for Morningstar. Our guest on the podcast today is Joseph Moore, a historian and author of the best-selling book How to Get Rich in American History, 300 years of financial advice that worked and didn't, where he chronicles all of the various things Americans have tried to do to get ahead over three centuries.
turns.zh: 我是Morningstar的个人理财与退休规划总监Christine Benz。今天请到的是历史学家Joseph Moore，他也是畅销书《How to Get Rich in American History》——讲的是三百年间灵光与不灵光的理财建议——书中记录了三百年来美国人为出人头地尝试过的各种路子。

turns.en: He's also an investor who went from being an academic to funding a tech startup, buying land on the moon, founding a cryptocurrency, and owning dozens of investment properties.
turns.zh: 他同时还是个投资人，从学者一路做到给科技初创公司投钱、在月球上买地、创建一种加密货币（cryptocurrency），还拥有几十处投资性房产。

turns.en: So, Christine, this was a really fun conversation where we covered a lot of ground about the history of financial advice in the U.S. as well as Joseph's own adventures in investing and money-making ventures.
turns.zh: Christine，这真是一场特别有意思的对话，我们聊了很多美国理财建议的历史，也聊了Joseph自己在投资和赚钱上的种种冒险。

turns.en: And one of the really interesting things he said, I thought, was that who you marry is actually a really strong indicator of financial success.
turns.zh: 我觉得他有个说法特别有意思：你嫁给谁，其实是财务成功一个很强的指标。

turns.en: I really like that part of the conversation too, Amy, as well as his discussion of the secret role of women in household financial decision-making.
turns.zh: 那段对话我也特别喜欢，Amy，还有他讲到女性在家庭财务决策里扮演的那个隐秘角色。

turns.en: I also thought Joseph's conversation of what he calls the despair industrial complex was incredibly thought-provoking. Yeah, those were all highlights for me too.
turns.zh: 我还觉得他谈的那个所谓的'绝望工业综合体'（despair industrial complex）特别发人深省。是啊，这些也都是我的高光时刻。

turns.en: All right, so let's roll the tape. Joseph, welcome to the long view. I am so excited to be here. Thank you for having me. Well, we're excited to have you.
turns.zh: 好，那我们来放正片。Joseph，欢迎参加The Long View。太荣幸来到这里，谢谢邀请。我们也高兴有你。

turns.en: You started out as a college professor, and I wanted to ask, how did you first get involved in real estate investing and writing about financial history, and what gave you the idea to write this book?
turns.zh: 你最早是大学历史教授。我想问问，你是怎么开始接触房产投资、开始写金融史的？写这本书的念头又是怎么来的？

turns.en: Dodging a bullet is the answer to that question. So, it's 2006, I think. My wife and I were graduate students, and back then the lesson of history supposedly was clear.
turns.zh: 躲过一颗子弹——这就是答案。应该是2006年，我和太太还是研究生。那时候'历史的教训'似乎很清楚。

turns.en: Everybody told you the lesson of history was renting, was throwing your money away. And instead of thinking about that like a historian, because I was literally getting a PhD in history as a graduate student, I nodded my head like everybody else did, and we got, we're both graduate students, and we got a no-income verification loan to buy a townhouse, which sounds as ridiculous today as it was then, but nobody thought it was ridiculous then.
turns.zh: 所有人都告诉你，历史的教训就是租房，买房就是往窗外扔钱。可我明明是在读历史博士，却没有像历史学家那样去想，而是跟所有人一样点点头就照做了。我们俩都是研究生，却办了一笔免收入核验贷款（no-income verification loan）买了栋联排别墅。这事今天听来荒唐，当时其实也一样荒唐，只不过当时没人觉得荒唐。

turns.en: Fast forward to 2008, our church offers a personal finance class for families. We went, they made us fill a budget, we go home. My wife goes to sleep, I did not sleep a wink.
turns.zh: 时间快进到2008年，我们教堂开了一门面向家庭的个人理财课。我们去上了，他们让我们填一份预算表，回到家，太太倒头就睡了，我一夜没合眼。

turns.en: I literally paced the house all night, because I was thinking, who gave us a mortgage? We have no business owning anything. We're graduate students.
turns.zh: 我在屋里走了一整晚，因为我在想：是谁给我们批的按揭？我们根本不具备拥有任何资产的资格，我们只是研究生啊。

turns.en: And so, we put our house on the market, it's sold on a Saturday, and the reason I remember the Saturday is because the following Saturday, our neighbor put her house on the market, and it never sold.
turns.zh: 于是我们把房子挂牌，一个周六卖掉了。我还记得那个周六，是因为下一个周六，我们邻居把她家也挂了牌，就再也没卖出去。

turns.en: So, it was the 2008 Titanic had sunk, and we were the last two people off of it. And I just kind of woke up intellectually and thought, why did I not think like a historian?
turns.zh: 2008年那艘泰坦尼克号沉了，我们是最后跳船的两个人。我那一下可以说是思想上彻底醒了：我为什么没有像历史学家那样思考？

turns.en: So, I had no business training whatsoever. But I wanted to come at this topic as a historian would to ask, what were people told to do? Did it work? And if so, what can we learn from that?
turns.zh: 我完全没有任何商业训练，但我想以历史学家的方式切入这个题目，去问：过去人们被告知该怎么做？有效吗？如果有效或者无效，我们能从中学到什么？

turns.en: And so, that began kind of an over a decade long journey of trying to find absolutely every scrap of financial advice I could discover in American history.
turns.zh: 就这样，开启了一段长达十几年的旅程：把美国历史上能找到的每一片理财建议的残篇断简都挖出来。

turns.en: And as it turns out, what everyone thought always worked was always changing. And so, in every generation, people finally feel like, well, we finally figured out finance and what to do to actually get ahead.
turns.zh: 结果发现，大家以为永远管用的东西其实一直在变。每一代人到最后都觉得，我们总算把财务搞明白了，知道该怎么真正出人头地了。

turns.en: And that it changes. And, you know, generation by generation, people have to adapt. And that's one of the things that you kind of take away from studying the past is we think the past is this stable thing.
turns.zh: 然后它就变了。一代又一代，人们都得不断适应。这也是研究历史给你的一个体会：我们以为过去是一个稳定的东西。

turns.en: And we are what moves through time. But the mean is moving behind you. And we can learn a lot by seeing how much change other generations had to endure.
turns.zh: 我们才是那个在时间里移动的东西，可你身后的基准一直在移动。看看其他世代不得不承受多大的变化，我们能学到很多。

turns.en: And, you know, I got lucky and endured that change on the right side of the 08 financial crisis. So we want to delve into some of the lessons that we can all learn from history.
turns.zh: 我运气不错，站在08年金融危机正确的这一边熬过了那次变动。所以我们很想深入谈谈历史能给我们所有人上的那几课。

turns.en: But we wanted to stick with your background a little bit. You decided to use what you know about history to make a million dollars. And you actually succeeded at that.
turns.zh: 不过我们想先在你的背景上多停留一会儿。你决定用你懂的历史去赚一百万美元，而且还真做到了。

turns.en: Did you always have a more practical bent than the typical academic? And I'm curious what people in your circle, your academic circle, thought about your money making efforts?
turns.zh: 你是不是天生就比一般学者更务实？我很好奇，你学术圈子里的人怎么看你这些赚钱的动作？

turns.en: Oh, no, they thought I was crazy, bluntly. So look, I have a lot of dear academic friends who kind of cross all ideological spectrums. But there is a tendency in academia, especially in the humanities where I reside, to think and talk very grandly about the working class.
turns.zh: 坦白说，他们觉得我疯了。你看，我有很多挚爱的学术朋友，跨越各种意识形态光谱。但学术界、尤其我所在的人文学科，有一种倾向：非常高调地谈论和书写工人阶级。

turns.en: Very few of the people who make such statements are actually from themselves, the working class. And I was raised in rural South Carolina. You know, I come from where the money was not found.
turns.zh: 可说这些话的人，自己来自工人阶级的寥寥无几。我是在南卡罗来纳乡下长大的，我来自那种和钱无缘的地方。

turns.en: Nobody in my family had money. I didn't know anybody. I didn't know a single person in my entire life until I probably was in my 30s who went to Ivy League school.
turns.zh: 我们家没一个人有钱。我长到三十多岁之前，这辈子认识的常春藤毕业生一个都没有。

turns.en: So like, there was just, this was a world apart from most academic backgrounds. I have a fun game I play with myself when I'm in academic conferences.
turns.zh: 所以这跟大多数学者的背景完全是两个世界。我在学术会议上会跟自己玩一个好玩的游戏。

turns.en: We're sitting around shooting the breeze, drinking a beer or something. And I'll ask people, where'd you go to high school? Because they're not ready for that question.
turns.zh: 大家围坐闲聊、喝杯啤酒什么的。我就问：你高中在哪儿读的？因为他们根本没防备这个问题。

turns.en: They are thinking, where'd you go to grad school? Where'd you do your undergrad? And so they'll just tell you, and I'll go look it up. And almost inevitably, it's like the most elite public education school or a preparatory academy somewhere.
turns.zh: 他们以为你要问研究生院或本科在哪儿读的，就照实答了，然后我去查。几乎无一例外，不是最顶尖的公立学校就是某所私立预备学院。

turns.en: And I'm like, don't you write books about the working class? But I can't, you know, my father used to climb underneath mobile homes and inspect electrical wire.
turns.zh: 我就想说，你们不是写工人阶级的书吗？可我不一样，我爸以前钻进活动板房底下检查电线。

turns.en: Like that was his job. He made $14,000 a year for a long time. And so I was just raised around the trades. I was raised around guys who, you know, did working class jobs and we had a working class life.
turns.zh: 那就是他的工作，有很长时间年薪一万四千美元。所以我从小就是在手艺行当里泡大的，周围都是干体力活的人，我们过的就是工薪阶层的生活。

turns.en: And it didn't occur to me to not have those values. And I remember when I got into academia, I was shocked because it was the first time I met people who would tell me, without thinking about it, that something was beneath them.
turns.zh: 我从没觉得那些价值观有什么不对。等我进了学术界反而震惊了，因为那是我第一次遇到会不假思索地说'这事太掉价、我不干'的人。

turns.en: Like, I wouldn't do that. That's beneath me. And I was like, something's, it had never occurred to me that something was beneath me to do. And so, yes, I do have a more practical bent, I think, than the average, especially humanities academic.
turns.zh: '我才不做那个，那太掉价了。'而我以前从来没想过还有'掉价'到不能做的事。所以，是的，我确实比一般的、尤其人文背景的学者更务实。

turns.en: And that led me to see things differently. And I think one of the, one of the things that's been a joy of his book tour is that in the world of finance, the reason my book is so different is that it, I didn't take any of the financial assumptions for granted that everyone just assumes are there.
turns.zh: 这让我看问题不一样。我觉得这次新书巡回的一个乐趣在于，在金融的世界里，我的书之所以如此不同，是因为大家默认存在的那些财务假设，我一个都没当成理所当然。

turns.en: I asked different questions. And from the academic perspective, it never occurred to me that those questions weren't worth asking. And hopefully that's led to a unique, a unique book. Certainly.
turns.zh: 我问了不一样的问题。从学术的角度看，我从来没觉得哪些问题不值得问。希望这成就了——一本独特的书。确实。

turns.en: It's been a crazy ride for me. Yeah, it definitely is unique and also very funny. So I really enjoyed reading it. Thank you. That was intentional. I really wanted it to be a fun read.
turns.zh: 对我来说这也是一段疯狂的旅程。是啊，它确实很独特，也特别好笑，我读得非常享受，谢谢。这是故意的，我就是想让它读起来好玩。

turns.en: I mean, I told somebody, I wanted to write a history of everyday people's finances that everyday people would enjoy reading. And so that's been one of the most rewarding things is hearing people say they enjoyed it, you know, that it's fun to read.
turns.zh: 我跟人说过，我想写一本讲普通人财务的历史，而且是普通人自己也爱读的那种。听到读者说他们喜欢、说读起来有趣，是最有回报的事之一。

turns.en: Because I remember when it was fun to read, so we need more books that are fun to read. Yeah, especially about finance. So one of the very first ideas you introduce in the book is the phrase go ahead.
turns.zh: 因为我记得读书本来是有趣的事，我们需要更多读起来有趣的书。是啊，尤其是讲理财的书。那么，书中最早提出的概念之一，就是'go ahead'这个短语。

turns.en: And you write that this was sort of like a 19th century Internet meme that meant moving to a better place than you began. Can you expand a little bit on what that phrase means and what makes this idea of going ahead uniquely American?
turns.zh: 你写道，它有点像19世纪的网络热梗（Internet meme），意思是去一个比你起点更好的地方。能展开讲讲这个短语的意思吗？为什么'go ahead'这个观念是美国独有的？

turns.en: Yeah, so the subtitle of the book is 300 years of financial advice that worked and didn't. And very few people have picked up on that. But the reason I did 300 years was that predates the American Revolution.
turns.zh: 好。这本书的副标题是'三百年间灵光与不灵光的理财建议'，很少有人注意到这一点。我之所以取三百年，是因为那要早于美国独立战争。

turns.en: And to some extent, what is the first uniquely American financial advice? And that advice is basically this. If you look around you in the poverty stricken town in which you live, England, Scotland, later Italy, parts of China, Japan.
turns.zh: 从某种意义上说，第一条真正美国独有的理财建议是什么？大意是这样的：如果你环顾自己身处的那个贫困小镇——英格兰、苏格兰，后来的意大利、中国部分地区、日本——

turns.en: If you will get on this rickety boat for roughly two months, then you can actually have a chance to get on the property ladder and move up with your life and go ahead from where you are to a better place.
turns.zh: 只要肯爬上那条摇摇晃晃的船漂上大约两个月，你就真的有机会踏上房产阶梯、让人生出息：从你所在的地方 go ahead，去一个更好的地方。

turns.en: And your children will have a chance to do the same. Now, that sounds inspiring, you know, on our side of the boat, but if you're on the other side of the boat, that's a risk reward proposition.
turns.zh: 你的孩子也有机会如法炮制。在我们这一头听来，这话很励志；可如果你站在船的那一头，这就是一笔风险与回报的权衡。

turns.en: It's not entirely clear it will work out. And to be clear, there are some people for whom it does not work out. Some of those boats didn't land in places that worked out.
turns.zh: 谁也不能保证一定成。说清楚点，有些人确实没成，有些船根本没靠上能出头的岸。

turns.en: But the idea that you could take a risk to move your family from a place that you would never get ahead to one where your family could actually see a better life at the end of yours was a uniquely American proposition at the time.
turns.zh: 但在当时，'愿意赌一把，把家人从一个永远出不了头的地方，搬到一个你这辈子结束时家人能看到更好生活的地方'——这个念头本身就是美国独有的。

turns.en: You had to actually get on the boat and do it. And so that idea pervades the 19th century especially. Now, people would talk about this in newspapers, in books, in bars.
turns.zh: 你得真的上船、真的去做。这个念头尤其弥漫了整个十九世纪。人们在报纸上、书里、酒吧里谈论它。

turns.en: Men, women, like people said, it's a go ahead culture. They commented on this over and we're a go ahead, not get ahead. We talk about getting ahead like it happens to you.
turns.zh: 男人女人都在说，这是个 go ahead 的文化。他们反复评论这一点——是 go ahead，不是 get ahead。我们说 get ahead，好像出人头地是发生在自己身上的事。

turns.en: But their assumption was that go ahead was something you had to get up and go do. And this crossed decades and the whole of the 1800s. It was a white idea, a black idea.
turns.zh: 可他们的假设是，go ahead 是你得起身去做的动作。这跨越了几十年，贯穿整个十九世纪。这是白人的观念，也是黑人的观念。

turns.en: I mean, Frederick Douglass, the famous abolitionist. We remember him mostly for his speech, What to the Slave is the Fourth of July, which is an incredible speech.
turns.zh: 比如著名废奴主义者Frederick Douglass。我们今天记住他，主要是因为那篇《What to the Slave is the Fourth of July》，确实是了不起的演讲。

turns.en: We teach it in schools. I've taught it. We should continue to teach it. But in his lifetime, that was even close to his most famous speech. Far and away, his most famous speech was called Self Made Men.
turns.zh: 我们学校里教，我也教过，应该继续教。但在他生前，那远算不上他最有名的演讲。遥遥领先、他最有名的演讲是《Self-Made Men》。

turns.en: And in that speech, now the gendered term there is just the term of the time he means men and women. But the idea of that speech, the crescendo line is maybe I cannot be president.
turns.zh: 那篇演讲里——当时那个性别化的词只是时代用语，他指的是男人和女人——整篇演讲的高潮大概是这句话：也许我当不了总统——

turns.en: He says as a black man in the 1870s, but I can be prosperous. And you have to think about like everywhere he went, white audiences and black audiences were calling out for that speech.
turns.zh: 他说，作为一个1870年代的黑人，但我可以发财致富。你想想，他无论走到哪儿，白人听众和黑人听众都在点名要听那篇演讲。

turns.en: And after he says I can be prosperous, he says our motto is go ahead. And that idea was pervasive and one that we've largely lost. We think getting ahead happens to you.
turns.zh: 说完'我可以发财'，他说：我们的座右铭就是 go ahead。这个观念曾经无处不在，如今我们大体已经丢了。我们以为出人头地是发生在自己身上的事。

turns.en: They thought that you happened to it. So a central idea of the book is that getting ahead or maybe going ahead is easier than ever. But we constantly see headlines about student debt, housing affordability, economic decline.
turns.zh: 他们以为是你朝着出人头地下手。本书的一个核心观点是：出人头地——或者该说 go ahead——比以往任何时候都容易。可我们天天看到的头条却是学生债务、住房负担、经济衰落。

turns.en: And I would say that statistics I've seen on economic mobility in the U.S. are pretty persuasive that it's not really what it once was. But maybe you can talk about that issue, why the media narrative is so negative and often it odds with historical evidence.
turns.zh: 我看过的一些关于美国经济流动性的统计，说实话相当有说服力地表明它今非昔比了。谈谈这个问题吧？为什么媒体叙事这么负面，而且常常和历史证据对不上？

turns.en: So there's kind of two ways we could take that conversation. One is the rhetorical conversation and one is the statistics. So let's do the rhetorical first.
turns.zh: 好。这个问题可以从两条线来聊：一条是修辞，一条是统计。先说修辞。

turns.en: Rhetorically, I can find people telling you the American dream is dead probably 300 years before I can find the actual phrase American dream, which comes up in the 1930s.
turns.zh: 从修辞上说，'美国梦已死'这种话，比'美国梦'这个词本身恐怕早出现三百年——那个词是1930年代才有的。

turns.en: So in the 1670s, this is 100 years before Hamilton is going to wrap on Broadway. In the 1670s, the colonists of Virginia burned their own capital to the ground in anger because no one could get ahead anymore.
turns.zh: 比如1670年代——那是Hamilton登上百老汇舞台的一百年前——1670年代，弗吉尼亚殖民地的居民一怒之下把自己的首府烧成白地，因为再也没人能出人头地了。

turns.en: That was from the very beginning. There's been rhetoric around no one's getting ahead. You arrive too late. There's big speeches in the 1800s saying this.
turns.zh: 从最开始就有'没人出头了'、'你来得太晚了'这种修辞。十九世纪就有著名的大演讲讲这些。

turns.en: One of my prized possessions is a 1984 bestselling book sold nearly 100,000 copies that said that the baby boomers would never be able to afford to retire.
turns.zh: 我的珍藏里有一本1984年的畅销书，卖了将近十万册，说的是婴儿潮一代永远都攒不够养老的钱。

turns.en: And so the rhetoric is very old. I call this big whoa, a kind of despair industrial complex because there's no clicks for a journalist. There's no votes for a politician.
turns.zh: 所以这套话术非常古老。我把这种big whoa式的悲情叫作'绝望工业综合体'（despair industrial complex），因为记者喊这个没有点击量，政客喊这个没有选票，

turns.en: Heck, there's no tenure for an academic like me if I just get up and tell everybody that the world is getting better. But I can have all of those things if I tell you it's getting worse.
turns.zh: 像我这样的学者，要是站起来告诉大家世界在变好，连终身教职都捞不到。可如果我告诉你它在变坏，这些东西我全都能有。

turns.en: So there's kind of the people who are giving that message out are actually being empowered by that message to implement their solutions or to monetize their traffic or whatever it is.
turns.zh: 所以那些散布坏消息的人，恰恰是被这个坏消息喂养的——靠它推行自己的解决方案，或者给自己的流量变现，诸如此类。

turns.en: But you actually end up getting penalized for listening because if you believe no one gets ahead, then you will not take the actions necessary to get ahead.
turns.zh: 但听信它的人反而会被惩罚：如果你相信没人出得了头，你就不会采取出人头地所需要的行动。

turns.en: So there's the rhetorical part of it. Let's move to the statistical part of it. There's two buckets of those mobility statistics. One of them is wrong and the other one I will take and use and flip on its head and show that it actually shows it's a lot better than you think it does.
turns.zh: 修辞的一面说完了，来看统计的一面。流动性统计分两拨：一拨是错的；另一拨我可以拿来用，而且倒过来一用，会发现它其实比你想的好得多。

turns.en: The first set of statistics that came out about mobility showed that the 1800s had this wildly rapid upward mobility in America and it's declined ever since.
turns.zh: 最早发布的那批流动性统计显示，十九世纪的美国有着极其迅猛的向上流动，此后一路下滑。

turns.en: The problem with those statistics is they were almost all taken from Iowa. The thing about Iowa is that it's not really representative of the whole of the United States.
turns.zh: 这些统计的问题在于，数据几乎全部取自爱荷华州。而爱荷华根本代表不了整个美国，

turns.en: It just happened to have a particularly good data set. And so a lot of the early mobility stats that celebrated how fast people could get ahead in the 1800s and early 20th century and then had the decline of it basically had forgotten about a lot of poor people, especially minorities who are just aren't in the data.
turns.zh: 它只是碰巧留有一套特别完整的数据集。所以很多早期流动性统计——歌颂十九世纪和二十世纪初人们出头有多快、然后又怎样衰落——基本把大量穷人、尤其少数族裔排除在数据之外了。

turns.en: And so when you combine the actual different demographic data sets, you find that mobility has gotten faster, not slower. Well, we forget how impoverished early Americans really were.
turns.zh: 当你真正把不同人口结构的数据集合并起来，你会发现流动性其实是变快了，不是变慢了。而且我们忘了早期的美国人到底有多穷。

turns.en: Then you look at something like the Ross Chetty famous paper in science that talks about, you know, basically mobility of Americans peaked for the generation born right after World War Two, that they got ahead of their parents faster than any generation and then it slows down after 1980.
turns.zh: 再看Raj Chetty那篇发表在《Science》上的著名论文，大致是说美国人的流动性在二战后紧跟着出生的那一代达到顶峰——他们超越父母的速度超过任何一代——1980年以后就慢下来。

turns.en: Okay, first of all, what they're really measuring is moving from the bottom to the middle class and for the chance to go from the bottom to the middle, that is probably true.
turns.zh: 第一，他们真正测的是从底层升入中产的机会。就'从底层到中层'这一点而言，恐怕是真的。

turns.en: However, their parents were living through the Great Depression. So this is a kind of skewed data set. This idea that like, well, my parents lived through the worst economic collapse in history and I'm doing pretty well.
turns.zh: 但那代人的父母正经历大萧条。所以这个数据集本身就带偏——'我父母经历过史上最糟的经济崩溃，而我混得还不错'这种比法，

turns.en: Is it necessary? It's, you know, the reality is the quality of life that we're living today absolutely dwarfs the quality of life of the early baby boomers.
turns.zh: 有什么意义呢？现实是，我们今天的生活质量，把婴儿潮早期一代的生活质量远远甩在身后。

turns.en: So when I look at that stat, I say, okay, what do we see? This is the Chetty data that I'm using. If you look at people born in the bottom fifth, six and 10 will get out in their own lifetime.
turns.zh: 所以我看那组数据时，我会问：我们看到了什么？这就是我用的Chetty的数据：出生在收入最低五分之一的人，6/10在自己的一生里能走出去。

turns.en: That is not perfect mobility, which would be eight and 10, but it's not that far off. Four and 10 make it to the middle class. One in 10 go all the way from the bottom all the way to the top.
turns.zh: 这不是完美的流动性——完美的应该是8/10——但也没差多远。4/10进入中产，1/10从最底层一直走到最顶层。

turns.en: That is compared to the rest of human history, mind blowing upward mobility. The flip side of that is downward mobility. Of children born in the top fifth, six and 10 will fall out in their own lifetime, which is the exact same as Denmark.
turns.zh: 放在整个人类历史的尺度上，这是惊人的向上流动。硬币的另一面是向下流动：出生在最高五分之一家庭的孩子，6/10会在自己的一生里跌出去——这和丹麦一模一样。

turns.en: So we have a rhetoric around mobility that is kind of skewed to the idea of one generation's experience. But when you pan the camera back out, you look over 300 years of history, Americans are getting ahead faster than our ancestors could have ever dreamed we could have.
turns.zh: 所以围绕流动性的那套修辞，其实是被一代人的特殊经历带偏了。把镜头拉远，放到三百年的历史尺度上看，美国人出人头地的速度，远超我们祖先敢想象的极限。

turns.en: You also note that your father hated rich people and it seems like that's sort of a growing attitude in the country now. We see lots of resentment toward the wealthy and interest in taxing billionaires, things like that.
turns.zh: 你还提到你父亲痛恨富人，而这种情绪如今在美国似乎越来越普遍。我们看到大量对富人的怨恨，还有对给亿万富翁征税的兴趣之类。

turns.en: Why has hostility toward wealth remained such a persistent part of American culture? So I think there's, I mean, that's a great question, by the way.
turns.zh: 为什么对财富的敌意一直是美国文化中如此持久的部分？我想——这真是个好问题。

turns.en: I don't want to pretend that I'm going to unlock that mystery in a couple of minutes, but I'd probably take it in two kind of general ideas.
turns.zh: 我不想假装几分钟就解开这个谜题，但我大概会从两个大的方面来谈。

turns.en: One is the kind of upward mobility motif that is the American dream or go ahead, as I used to say. There was an empowerment of people at the bottom that was very unusual compared to any other place in the world at the time.
turns.zh: 一个是向上流动这个母题——美国梦，或者用我的说法，go ahead。它赋予了底层人民一种力量，这在当时的世界上是极其罕见的。

turns.en: And that gave people a voice to decry anything. I mean, the free press may be honestly part of the answer. Just the idea that you lived in a nation where such opinions could be freely expressed without fear of retribution from said elites and rich people was somewhat unique.
turns.zh: 这让人们敢于谴责任何事情。说真的，新闻自由恐怕就是答案的一部分。生活在一个这种观点可以自由表达、不必担心权贵报复的国家，这个观念本身就与众不同。

turns.en: And so the ability to print those ideas and those complaints, there may have been those complaints for all of history, but you can't read them very often.
turns.zh: 于是这些想法、这些抱怨能被印出来。抱怨恐怕有史以来都有，只是你平时读不到它们。

turns.en: I mean, you get the levelers in England and these, but that's not common. But I think the other thing, the reason that we seem to think it's getting more loud today.
turns.zh: 英格兰的掘地派（the levelers）算一个，但那是少数。而我想到另一层——为什么我们觉得今天这种声音越来越响。

turns.en: I think we probably misjudge how local life used to be and how national media landscape has become in the sense that most people's experience with the rich was local.
turns.zh: 我想我们多半低估了过去生活的'地方性'，也低估了媒体格局变得多么'全国化'。以前大多数人对富人的体验是本地化的，

turns.en: It was the local elites that they knew. They may know the Rockefellers exist, but they've never met one. They've never walked past their Park Avenue homes and had to like gawk at them and wonder why they have to live in a tiny apartment.
turns.zh: 他们认识的是本地精英。他们也许知道Rockefeller家族的存在，但从没见过任何一个Rockefeller。他们不会路过Park Avenue上的豪宅瞪眼张望，纳闷自己为什么只能住小公寓。

turns.en: Some New Yorkers might, but most people in the country are living a very local life. And now we have a very nationalized media. And so if you go over to the previous time that we have an explosion of kind of critiques of wealth from a kind of socialist perspective, the way we're seeing now.
turns.zh: 有些纽约人也许会，但全国大多数人过着很本地化的生活。而现在我们的媒体高度全国化了。上一次我们看到这种从类社会主义视角出发、对财富的大爆发式批判——就像现在这样的——

turns.en: The last time was around the presidency of Eugene Debs and kind of started with the populist angst about the railroads. Well, what was happening with railroads and radio is an era in which we're nationalizing our economy and our media.
turns.zh: 是Eugene Debs竞选总统前后，起点是民粹主义者对铁路的怨气。铁路和无线电那个年代，正是我们的经济和媒体走向全国化的年代。

turns.en: So anytime local people are suddenly confronted with narratives about national elites that they'll I've never met Elon Musk and probably never will probably won't see him with my own eyes.
turns.zh: 所以每当本地人突然被抛在全国精英的叙事面前——我从来没见过Elon Musk，以后大概也不会亲眼见到他——

turns.en: But I'm very aware of him in a way I would not be if my media consumption and my life was entirely local. And most people's lives generally were.
turns.zh: 可我对他再熟悉不过，而如果我的媒体消费和生活完全局限于本地，我不会这样。而过去大多数人的人生，通常就完全是本地化的。

turns.en: One of the books main ideas is you live most of your life in slow time and that's a quote you get rich and fast time. Maybe you could talk a bit more about what that means.
turns.zh: 书的另一个主要观点是：你人生的大部分时间活在'慢时间'（slow time）里，而你变富是在'快时间'（fast time）里。能再讲讲这是什么意思吗？

turns.en: So most of us don't think a lot about financial history. It's not it's not top of mind for most of us. We wake up in the morning. If we ever think about financial history at all, almost certainly it's what I call fast time history.
turns.zh: 好。我们大多数人不太去想金融史，它不在我们心头。早上醒来，要是偶尔想起金融史，那几乎一定是我所说的快时间历史。

turns.en: That's when everything is changing everywhere all at once to quote the movie and a handful of smart people saw it coming. Everybody else got wiped out and you just don't want to be the dumb people.
turns.zh: 就是借用那部片子的说法：所有地方的一切同时在变，一小撮聪明人看出了苗头，其他人都被扫荡殆尽——你就是不想当那个傻子。

turns.en: It's always 1929. It's always 2008. And the problem with those histories is not that they're not good and fun. They are. But they're not written to teach you what to do with your money.
turns.zh: 永远是1929，永远是2008。这类历史的问题不在于不好看、不好玩——它们很好看——而在于它们不是为教你怎么打理自己的钱而写的。

turns.en: They are written to entertain you and they're very good at that. Like you are supposed to flip the page or look at the movie screen and scream, you know, he's behind you.
turns.zh: 它们是写给娱乐你的，而且非常在行。你就应该翻着书页、盯着银幕尖叫：他在你身后！

turns.en: The subprime mortgage lender is behind you run away from the mortgage. That's what you're supposed to do with those histories and they're very good at that.
turns.zh: 次级房贷机构在你身后，快逃离房贷！——这就是这类历史要你做的，它们这方面做得特别好。

turns.en: But they're not there to teach you what to actually do with your money because most of financial history is not fast time. Most change is slow and imperceptible.
turns.zh: 但它们不是来教你实际该怎么打理钱财的，因为金融史的大部分时间不是快时间。大多数变化是缓慢的、难以察觉的。

turns.en: And by the way, that doesn't mean it's quiet. It could be very loud in fast time. One of my favorite things to do when I'm giving public talks, I go around like I give talks and, you know, different organizations or whatever.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这不意味着安静。在快时间里可以非常喧嚣。我做公开演讲时最喜欢玩的一个环节是——我去各种机构演讲——

turns.en: And I will put on the screen two quotes from the New York Times. And one essentially says a depression is right around the corner. And one says a booming economy is right around the corner.
turns.zh: 我在屏幕上放两条《New York Times》的话。一条大意是大萧条近在眼前，另一条大意是繁荣经济近在眼前。

turns.en: And I tell people these are less than three months apart. Headlines of the New York Times. Now, guess the year. And people will, you know, hands go up 1939, 19, you know, 2007, 2008, 1929, 1930.
turns.zh: 然后我告诉大家，这两条《New York Times》标题相隔不到三个月，猜猜是哪年？人们举手抢答：1939、19年……2007、2008、1929、1930。

turns.en: I tell them it's 1948. And then I ask if anyone can remember anything that happened in 1948. And usually most people cannot because it was a very boring historical year, especially for markets.
turns.zh: 我告诉他们：1948年。然后我问谁还记得1948年发生过什么。多数人答不上来，因为那在历史上是非常无聊的一年，尤其对市场而言。

turns.en: And yet people were screaming in the headlines that boom or bust was right around the corner. So slow time can be very loud. But most of your life is lived with people being loud and volatility kind of staying within a normal range.
turns.zh: 可当时人们却在头版上声嘶力竭地喊：要么繁荣、要么崩盘，就在眼前。所以慢时间也可以很喧嚣。但你人生的大部分，就是在人们大声嚷嚷、波动率大致处于正常区间的状态中度过的。

turns.en: And that's where most of your financial life will be lived. That's where most of your financial decisions will be made. And it's the decisions you make in slow time that can be stress tested in fast time.
turns.zh: 你的财务生活主要在那里度过，你的财务决策大多在那里做出。正是在慢时间里做出的决定，才经得起快时间的压力测试。

turns.en: And people usually leap ahead in fast time. Any business owner knows this. They'll have a phrase something like you work and you work and you work and nothing happens and then out of nowhere everything breaks.
turns.zh: 人通常是在快时间里跳跃前进的。任何生意人都懂，他们常说类似的话：你干啊干啊干，什么都没发生，然后平地一声雷，全塌了。

turns.en: And that's most financial life. You also argue that people should take more risks. What kind of risks are actually worth taking? Yeah. So let's first of all, let's define risk because some people can hear that and think, you know, put out a HELOC on the house and put it all on Bitcoin, which is gambling.
turns.zh: 财务人生的大半就是这样。你还主张人们应该多冒点险。到底哪些风险值得冒？是的。首先我们把风险定义清楚，因为有人听了可能会想：那就拿房子做一笔房屋净值信贷额度（HELOC），全押比特币——那叫赌博。

turns.en: And the difference between gambling and risk could be summarized simply as do you have some measurable impact on the outcome? You know, I can't affect the price of Bitcoin.
turns.zh: 赌博和风险的差别可以简单归结为一句话：你对结果有没有可衡量的影响？我影响不了比特币的价格。

turns.en: Nothing I'm going to do will shake it. But I can have some measurable impact on a whole lot of other risks that I take, whether it's an investment property that I'm going to turn around, whether it's an investment in a small business that I'm going to, you know, run better.
turns.zh: 我怎么做都撼动不了它。但我承担的很多其他风险，我都能施加可衡量的影响——不管是我打算盘活的一处投资性房产，还是我要经营得更好的一笔小企业投资，

turns.en: Whether it's a rearrangement of my investment portfolio so that I'm putting away more money than I otherwise would. But like if I have some control over what's happening, then at least it's a risk, not a gamble.
turns.zh: 还是我重新调整投资组合，让自己存下的钱比本来更多。只要我对事态有一定掌控，那至少算风险，不是赌博。

turns.en: And I think most risks, if you go back through history, the idea that most of your risks worth taking were all in the market would have not made any sense to anyone.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得，往回看历史，'值得冒的风险大部分在市场里'这个观念，过去任何人都不会认同。

turns.en: Even business leaders would not have understood that. Most of your risks were going to be in your business or your career. One of the things I think people can misread in much of the literature, including in my book, you've got to be careful, is I'm not saying quit your job and go start a small business and risk it all there.
turns.zh: 连企业家都理解不了。你的大部分风险本该在你的生意或你的职业里。人们在很多文献——包括我这本书里——容易误读的一点是，你得当心：我不是说让你辞了工作去开小企业、把一切押上去。

turns.en: There's ways to risk in business and there's ways to risk inside of another business, like taking a salary from somebody else's business. But what I think has happened in the course of the last four to five decades is because the baby boomers have had such a wild, successful run of having their retirement savings make them rich, we have assumed that the way you get rich is by slowly steadily putting money away in low-risk assets.
turns.zh: 在生意里冒险是一种方式，在别人的生意里冒险也是一种方式，比如在别人的公司领一份工资。但我觉得过去四五十年发生的是：婴儿潮一代的退休储蓄运气好得离谱、把他们送进了富有行列，于是我们默认发家之道就是细水长流地把钱投进低风险资产。

turns.en: That usually did not work in history. So the risks we're taking, the first one is in your career. You know, when young people, if I'll talk to young people and they'll say, you know, should I be putting $100, $200 a month away in the stock market?
turns.zh: 这在历史上通常行不通。我们该冒的风险，第一个在职业里。年轻人来找我，说：我该每月往股市里投一百、两百美元吗？

turns.en: Sure, sounds like a great idea. But just a quick question, is there a credential that you could go get that would help you in the next five years double your salary?
turns.zh: 投呗，好主意。但我就问一句：有没有一项证书，你拿下之后能在未来五年让薪水翻倍？

turns.en: Put your money on that. I mean, I met a guy researching the book who's never been to college, makes a fabulous salary because he's gotten every credential in the industry for airline mechanics.
turns.zh: 把钱押在那上面。我写书调研时认识一个人，大学都没上过，收入却高得离谱，因为他把航空机务行业的所有执业认证考了个遍。

turns.en: And you literally can't take the plane apart and put it back together, which you have to do every so many miles unless he signs off on it. He's doing great because he invested in his career.
turns.zh: 飞机拆开再装回去——每隔一定飞行里程必须做的那种检修——没有他签字根本不行。他现在混得很好，因为他投资了自己的职业。

turns.en: There's a big difference in the income of an entry-level nurse and a nurse anesthetist. And so, first and foremost, invest in your career, invest in getting better and better so that your income can grow by an exponent.
turns.zh: 入门级护士和麻醉护士（nurse anesthetist）的收入差距很大。所以，首先也是最重要的，投资你的职业，投资让自己越来越强，好让你的收入成倍增长。

turns.en: But then there's small business. I mean, that really is one of the ways most deco-millionaires and above got to that point was by owning, investing in a small business.
turns.zh: 再就是小企业。我是说，绝大多数千万富豪（decamillionaires）及以上身家的人走到那一步，靠的正是拥有或投资小企业。

turns.en: And we have more such deco-millionaires and above than we've ever had in American history, even adjusted for inflation, by the way. And most of those people are doing very un-sexy jobs in industries you've never thought of.
turns.zh: 顺便说，我们拥有的千万富豪及以上的人，比美国历史上任何时候都多，哪怕按通胀调整也一样。而且他们中的多数人做的活儿一点都不性感，所在的行业你根本想不到。

turns.en: Like, the Wall Street Journal ran a thing on these men and women who were doing this, one of whom has a carpet removal company specializing in over-the-summer carpet removal.
turns.zh: 《Wall Street Journal》报道过一批做这类生意的男男女女，其中一位经营地毯拆除公司，专攻暑期学校地毯拆除。

turns.en: Because schools, when they need new carpet, they've got like 60 days max to pull that off. And you've got a whole school. And he's just specialized in removing carpet for schools.
turns.zh: 因为学校要换地毯，最多六十天窗口要完工，而且是整所学校。他就专门给学校拆地毯。

turns.en: And he's, you know, worth 10 million. And I've interviewed so many people like this in research in the book who are doing things you would have never thought to do.
turns.zh: 他身家一千万。我写书过程中访谈过太多这样的人，做着你想都想不到的事。

turns.en: So take the risk in your own career, in small business. I think those are risks we're taking. So if most wealth is created in occasional bursts rather than a steady march upward, how should investors position themselves for those fast-time moments?
turns.zh: 所以，在自己的职业里冒险，在小生意上冒险，我认为这些才是我们在冒的风险。那么，既然大部分财富是在偶发的爆发而非稳步上行中创造的，投资人该如何为那些快时间时刻布局？

turns.en: So that's a great question, too. I'm working on an essay on this from my sub-stack right now. I have it wrestled down, but I want to make it interesting and fun to read.
turns.zh: 这也是个好问题。我正在Substack上写一篇关于这个的文章，内容已经成稿，但我想把它写得有趣好读。

turns.en: So that's the part. How do you make social sciences equations fun to read? It's not always an easy circle to square. But it basically boils down to this.
turns.zh: 难就难在这儿——怎么让社会科学的公式读起来有意思？这不是件容易圆回来的事。但核心归结起来是这么回事。

turns.en: The equation is going to look something like this. You're going to have volatility, which you can't predict. You're going to have concentration of assets, which you control.
turns.zh: 公式大概长这样：一个是波动率，你预测不了；一个是资产集中度，这个你说了算。

turns.en: You decide how concentrated your risk profile is. And then the other things you can control outside of that is how much liquidity do you have against how urgent are your debt deadlines?
turns.zh: 你的风险敞口有多集中，由你决定。除此之外你能控制的是：手上有多少流动性，以及你的债务期限有多急。

turns.en: Not the amount of debt you have, but the payment schedule for that debt. And people who are in different industries know that debt works very differently in different industries.
turns.zh: 关键不是你欠多少，而是那笔债的还款时间表。身处不同行业的人都知道，债务在不同行业里玩法完全不同。

turns.en: If you have a lot of debt, but it's all in 3.5% mortgages on rental properties, your debt deadlines are pretty easy to manage. If you've got a balloon note coming due in 18 months, that is much harder to manage.
turns.zh: 如果你债很多，但都是3.5%利率的出租房按揭，债务到期压力很好管理。可如果有一笔气球贷（balloon note）18个月后到期，那就难管得多。

turns.en: So if fast time hits when you have a low liquidity and a looming debt deadline, you can get wiped out quickly. And so needing to manage the liquidity versus the deadlines for your debt is one part of that.
turns.zh: 所以，如果快时间降临时你流动性很低、债务到期又步步紧逼，你会很快被清出局。管好流动性与债务到期日之间的关系，是布局的一环。

turns.en: But the other part is the concentration. Fast time rewards and punishes concentration. So when fast time comes, when everything shifts, the people who are concentrated in the areas that it's in are the ones who outperform everyone else.
turns.zh: 另一环是集中度。快时间奖励集中，也惩罚集中。当快时间到来、一切切换的时候，恰好重仓在受益领域的人，会跑赢所有人。

turns.en: Because of the concentration when everything shifted. And of course, the same thing to the downside. And so you have to think very strategically about where do I want to be concentrated when change comes.
turns.zh: 就是因为切换时他们集中在那里。当然，往下跌的时候也一样。所以你得非常有策略地想：变化来临时，我想重仓在哪里？

turns.en: And when that change comes, especially if it comes in the way I wasn't expecting, can I survive it by looking at the relationship to my liquidity and the debt deadlines that I have to carry?
turns.zh: 而当变化真的来了——尤其以你没预料到的方式来了——你要能靠审视流动性与所背负债务到期日之间的关系而活下来。

turns.en: And now that's, again, you can see why it's a struggle to make that essay fun to read. But you just have to understand that financial time and regular time don't work on the same speed.
turns.zh: 你看，这就是为什么那篇文章很难写得有趣。但你必须明白：财务时间和日常时间不在同一个速度上运转。

turns.en: So imagine I put on your wrist a regular, perfectly timed wristwatch. And then I take another clock and I take it to the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.
turns.zh: 想象我给你腕上戴一只走时分毫不差的手表，再拿另一只钟放到纽约证券交易所的交易大厅里。

turns.en: The one on your wrist is going to tick with everyone else's time. But the one on the stock exchange is going to tick for every normal second of financial activity.
turns.zh: 你手腕上那只和大家的时间一起滴答；但交易所那只，会按金融活动的节奏滴答。

turns.en: On the average month, the clock on your wrist and the clock on the stock exchange are going to roughly, you know, they're going to align pretty well.
turns.zh: 在平均水平的月份里，你腕上的钟和交易所的钟大致是——基本——对得上的。

turns.en: Because there's an average month with an average amount of up and down. And so they're going to stay aligned. But every now and again, that clock on the stock exchange speeds up incredibly or goes backwards.
turns.zh: 因为平均月里涨跌也平均，两个钟保持同步。可隔三差五，交易所那只钟会骤然加速，甚至倒着走。

turns.en: And so financial time can operate at a different speed than the time of the life you're living. And so you want to be concentrated in the right places when that happens.
turns.zh: 所以财务时间可以和你人生的时间以不同速度运转。当那一刻来临，你要保证自己恰好重仓在对的地方；

turns.en: And you want to be able to survive it if you're concentrated in the wrong places. We also wanted to ask you a couple of questions about the history of financial advice, which you also cover in the book.
turns.zh: 而如果重仓错了地方，你也得能活下来。关于理财建议这门行业的历史——你书里也讲到——我们还想请教你几个问题。

turns.en: And you argue that financial advice as a profession emerged almost accidentally. There was no job title of financial advisor before 1969. Can you talk about how the profession of financial advice first got started?
turns.zh: 你提出，理财建议作为一门职业几乎是在偶然中诞生的。1969年之前根本没有 financial advisor 这个职位名称。能讲讲这个行业最初是怎么起步的吗？

turns.en: Yeah, so let's go before the dawn of modern financial industry. Where was most financial advice found? And this surprised me because the trail went cold for me as a historian.
turns.zh: 好，我们回到现代金融行业诞生之前。那时候理财建议主要藏在哪儿？这个答案让我都意外——对一个历史学者来说，线索一度断了。

turns.en: I'm basically a detective. I'm reading Dead People's Mail trying to figure out what happened. And the trail went cold right around 1910, 1912, where I ended up finding most financial advice before then was in housewife manuals.
turns.zh: 我本质上是个侦探，靠读死者的信件还原发生了什么。线索大约断在1910、1912年前后——在那之前，我发现最多的理财建议竟然写在'家庭主妇手册'（housewife manuals）里。

turns.en: Because the average housewife has to manage the whole family's income and out go. Women's magazines are replete with financial advertisements for mortgage companies or investment opportunities.
turns.zh: 因为普通主妇要操持全家的收入与支出。女性杂志上登满了按揭公司和投资机会的广告。

turns.en: So like women were really active in forming financial ideas and executing them. And that's a part of history that's been completely lost. Then something happens in 1912.
turns.zh: 所以女性其实非常活跃地参与形成并执行理财观念。这是一段彻底失落的历史。然后1912年，有事发生了。

turns.en: All financial advice before 1912 was kind of easy to understand. Everyone knew what to do. And that basically boiled down to, you know, if you were going to have paper investments, you wanted to invest in bonds or dividend yielding stocks at about 5% because there was 0% inflation.
turns.zh: 1912年之前的理财建议都挺好懂，人人知道该怎么做，归结起来就是：如果要持有纸面投资，就买债券或股息率约5%的分红股票，因为通胀是0%。

turns.en: And then in 1912, when there's 0% inflation, everything changes. Inflation goes from zero. So 1912, a gallon of milk costs 24 cents a gallon.
turns.zh: 然后在通胀为0的1912年，一切都变了。通胀从零起飞。1912年，一加仑牛奶24美分。

turns.en: If I go back in time to 1812, think about 1812 to 1912. In 1812, Napoleon rules France and men wear hoes. Like that's a different world than 1912.
turns.zh: 如果把时间拨回1812年——想想1812到1912——1812年，Napoleon统治法国，男人穿长筒袜（hose）。那和1912年完全是两个世界。

turns.en: And in 1912, inflation goes from 0% to the next year it goes 8, which is double where we are right now. 8, 18, 17, 17, 15 in five years. Prices doubled.
turns.zh: 1912年之后，通胀从0%起跳，第二年就到8%——正好是我们现在水平的两倍——8%、18%、17%、17%、15%，五年之间物价翻倍。

turns.en: There was not a mother, a grandmother or a great grandmother who knew what to do. And everything that used to work stopped working. And all the things that you used to be told not to do, like invest in stocks, started to work.
turns.zh: 没有任何一位母亲、祖母或曾祖母知道该怎么办。过去一切管用的都不管用了，过去劝你别做的事——比如买股票——反倒管用了。

turns.en: And so there's this explosion of financial literature in the 1910s and 20s about how to understand this new world and what to do. But there's really not anybody to turn to who has mastered this and kind of codified it into a job description where they help you.
turns.zh: 于是1910、1920年代理财读物井喷，都在讲如何理解这个新世界、该怎么做。但确实没有人真正吃透这一切、把它编成一份助人的职位描述。

turns.en: You can go to your banker and they can help you execute some things. You can go to a broker, but most people don't have brokers and most people don't buy stocks.
turns.zh: 你可以找银行家帮你执行一些操作，可以找经纪人，但多数人没有经纪人，多数人也不买股票。

turns.en: That starts to shift in the 1960s. Most people's financial purchases were one of two things. If it was a market or put aside real estate, which was actually what most people spent their money on or invested their money with.
turns.zh: 这个局面从1960年代开始转变。多数人的金融购买无非两类：要么市场，要么房地产——而房地产才是多数人真正把钱花上、投上的地方。

turns.en: But let's go to the paper investments. It was mutual funds and insurance. That's what most people did. And in the late 1960s, there were all kinds of scandals about just how egregious some of the sales techniques were for basically selling insurance products that were mostly good for the insurance company and selling mutual funds with huge fees.
turns.zh: 再说纸面投资，普通人买的就是共同基金（mutual funds）和保险。1960年代末冒出各种丑闻，讲销售手法有多恶劣：卖那些主要对保险公司有利的保险产品，收着天价费用的共同基金。

turns.en: I mean, fees that would make mutual fund advisors today feel embarrassed if they got. And while that was great for the industry, it was bad for the average consumer and a group of mutual fund salesmen and insurance salesmen agree to have a meeting at the Chicago O'Hare Airport.
turns.zh: 那种费用率，今天的共同基金顾问拿到都会脸红。这繁荣了行业，却害了普通消费者。于是，一群共同基金销售员和保险销售员约在芝加哥O'Hare机场开了个会。

turns.en: And I can't remember exactly how many. It's not many. It's maybe a dozen or so people fly in. These are like the top selling mutual fund and insurance salesmen in the country.
turns.zh: 具体人数记不清了，人不多，大概十几个人飞过去。这些都是全美最顶尖的基金和保险销售员。

turns.en: And they all feel like this industry is kind of getting rotten and they don't want to be associated with that. So they fly in, they have a meeting and they decide we're going to find a new entity, a nonprofit that's going to be financial advising.
turns.zh: 都觉得这行在腐烂，不想跟这名声沾边。于是他们飞过去、开了会，决定成立一个新主体——一个非营利机构——来做财务建议这件事。

turns.en: So they fly in as insurance salesmen and mutual fund salesmen. And they never leave O'Hare, by the way. And then they fly out and they're financial advisors.
turns.zh: 他们飞进去时是保险销售员、基金销售员。顺便说，他们压根没离开O'Hare机场。飞出来的时候，身份就变成了理财顾问。

turns.en: They change their title in that meeting. And going forward, that idea spreads that you could have certified financial planners or financial advisors, different groups spring up to do it.
turns.zh: 头衔就在那场会上改了。从那以后，'可以有注册理财规划师（certified financial planner）或理财顾问'这个理念扩散开，各种机构纷纷成立来做这件事。

turns.en: But that's a new thing in the 60s. And in a way, I argue it's actually a really good thing. Because prior to that, you couldn't really find anybody in your local community who could help you understand all of these different financial investments all at the same time.
turns.zh: 这是1960年代才有的新事物。某种程度上，我认为它其实是大好事。因为在此之前，你在本地社区根本找不到能同时帮你弄懂所有这些不同金融产品的人。

turns.en: So it's a new profession because it's an entirely new investing world. You write in the book that Dave Ramsey has changed more people's personal finances than maybe anyone in history.
turns.zh: 所以这是一门新职业，对应的是一个全新的投资世界。你在书里写，Dave Ramsey改变的个人财务也许比历史上任何人都多。

turns.en: So why do academics and financial experts tend to look down on figures like Ramsey? Well, I've always loved Morningstar. So something tells me that the Morningstar audience is not going to like that.
turns.zh: 那为什么学界和金融专业人士往往看不起Ramsey这类人物？我一直很喜欢Morningstar，所以我猜Morningstar的听众大概不会喜欢我接下来说的。

turns.en: You've got some very sophisticated financial listeners out there. So let me make my case for why gurus get a bad rap, especially amongst professionals.
turns.zh: 你们的听众金融素养很高。那就让我为'理财大师们'辩几句，说说他们为什么名声不好，尤其在专业人士眼里。

turns.en: Finance professors have incredible equations that work very well on spreadsheets. What gurus have is the awareness that Superbowl adds work.
turns.zh: 金融教授有很厉害的公式，在电子表格里跑得很好。大师们掌握的却是'超级碗广告管用'这种直觉。

turns.en: Birthday sex leads to baby number three. And I have yet to see a finance equation that models accurately a midlife crisis or a child with special needs.
turns.zh: 生日当晚行房，就会生出老三。可我至今没见过哪个金融公式能准确给中年危机或有特殊需求的孩子建模。

turns.en: When you live in the real world and it's dynamic and changing, you need some rules of thumb. And what you find when you look at studies of what people who read personal finance gurus actually remember, it's not what's in the book.
turns.zh: 当你活在真实、动态、不断变化的世界里，你需要一些经验法则。去看'读者实际记住了什么'的研究，你会发现他们记住的不是书里的内容本身。

turns.en: It's what do you remember from the book? And if I go to the average person who read a finance guru, let's just pick one off the shelf that's particularly egregious, Rich Dad Poor Dad, which I think we can all agree is an eye roll level book.
turns.zh: 而是'你还记得书里讲了什么'。如果我问一个读过理财大师书的普通人——随便挑一本特别离谱的：《Rich Dad Poor Dad》，我们都同意那是让人翻白眼的书——

turns.en: But the average person only remembers that they should buy assets and that assets are defined very simply as things that make you money instead of cost you money.
turns.zh: 普通人只记住了：要买资产；而资产被简单定义为给你进钱、而不是从你兜里掏钱的东西。

turns.en: That's what they actually remember. Now, as a thing to remember, that's not such a bad thing. And so if you look at the way people read gurus versus what gurus say, there's a disparity.
turns.zh: 这就是他们实际记住的。作为一条要记住的原则，这还真不坏。所以，人们读大师的方式和大师所说的内容之间，存在一个落差。

turns.en: And that disparity really matters. So let's look at Dave Ramsey. And every single academic discipline has a paper somewhere in a journal. And I'm not making this hypothetically.
turns.zh: 这个落差非常重要。来看Dave Ramsey。几乎每个学科在期刊的某个角落都有一篇批判他的论文——我不是假设——

turns.en: I have read these papers that condemns Dave Ramsey. Sociology, women's and gender studies, history, finance, economics. They all have an anti-Dave Ramsey paper somewhere.
turns.zh: 我确实读过这些批判Dave Ramsey的论文。社会学、女性与性别研究、历史、金融、经济学，每个学科都藏着一篇'反Ramsey'论文。

turns.en: And sure, there's plenty of things that Dave Ramsey says that I could disagree with. But a German economics student who did not have a dog in the fight, who was just looking for an interesting thesis to write, I think it was his PhD thesis, had the idea to overlay credit card balances with where the Ramsey show, which was an AM radio show through the 90s and 2000s, would show up in a new market.
turns.zh: 当然，Ramsey的很多说法我也可以不同意。但有一个德国经济学学生，跟这事没有利害关系，只是想找个有趣的题目——我记得那是他的博士论文——他的点子是：把信用卡余额数据，和Ramsey节目（那是90年代和2000年代一档AM电台节目）进入新市场的时点叠加起来。

turns.en: In other words, when a new radio station would pick the show up, did it change anything? Lo and behold, credit card spinning went down in that metro 1.3%.
turns.zh: 换句话说，当一个新的电台开始播这个节目，情况有变化吗？果不其然，那个都市区的信用卡周转透支（churning）下降了1.3%。

turns.en: Well, how do you know correlation is not causation or all those things? He has the idea to realize AM radio waves cannot penetrate mountains.
turns.zh: 那怎么确定相关不是因果呢？他的巧思在于：AM无线电波穿不过山脉。

turns.en: Therefore, the zip codes on the other side of mountain ranges won't get the show. They won't get the signal. And sure enough, the credit card spending data there stays the same.
turns.zh: 于是山脉另一侧的邮编区域收不到这个节目、收不到信号。果然，那一带的信用卡消费数据纹丝不动。

turns.en: So if you do the math on that, which I have, that means that over the course of his life, Dave Ramsey has saved the American economy, the GDP of a midsize nation state, just by yelling at people to sell the car.
turns.zh: 把这笔账算下来——我算过——就意味着Dave Ramsey这辈子凭一己之力为美国经济省下了相当于一个中等国家GDP的钱——仅仅靠冲着人们喊'把那辆车卖了'。

turns.en: Now, you can agree or disagree with the finer points of his ideas, but I challenge you to prove that you could save the American economy, the GDP of a midsize nation state, and then concentrate most of those benefits to average working class Americans.
turns.zh: 你可以对他的具体观点同意或不同意，但我请你证明自己也能拯救美国经济、省出一个中等国家的GDP，还把大部分好处落到普通工薪阶层美国人头上。

turns.en: That's a pretty hard trick to pull off. And so if you step back and ask what is the effect of these folks versus what is the image of them as TikTok gurus selling scammy courses, they've actually had quite a big impact for the good.
turns.zh: 这可太难做到了。所以你退一步问：这些人的实际效果，对比他们作为TikTok大师卖割韭菜课程的形象，其实他们带来了相当大的善果。

turns.en: Now, I tell people, don't buy their seminars. Just everything they say that's good is usually for free. And so you don't need to do much more than take what's for free.
turns.zh: 我常告诉大家：别买他们的收费讲座。他们讲的东西，好的部分基本都是免费的。你只要把免费的部分拿走就够了。

turns.en: You talked at the beginning about your first experience buying real estate and getting a loan right before the financial crisis. We also wanted to touch on some of your other adventures in investing.
turns.zh: 你在节目开头讲了金融危机前夕你第一次买房、贷款的经历。我们也想聊聊你其他一些投资冒险。

turns.en: You once invested in West Coast startup that developed technology to help ALS patients communicate, but you ended up losing your entire investment.
turns.zh: 你曾投资西海岸一家初创公司，做帮助渐冻症（ALS）患者沟通的技术，结果你把投资全部亏光了。

turns.en: What lesson did you take away from that experience? Well, from that one in particular, and I just have so much admiration for the young people who started that business, but what it took away was it's really hard to have a successful business.
turns.zh: 那次经历让你学到了什么？就那一件而言——我非常敬佩创办那家公司的年轻人——但它让我明白的是：做成一门生意真的很难。

turns.en: Like, successful business is hard. And anyone listening to this who's run a business understands that. Anyone who's, you know, I was joking with somebody recently.
turns.zh: 成功的生意就是难。听这期节目里凡是经营过生意的人都懂。前阵子有个人跟我打趣，问——

turns.en: They said, what turns you from a lefty humanities professor to a kind of moderate, conservative, kind of pro-capitalism guy? And I said, making payroll.
turns.zh: 他说，是什么把你从一个左翼人文学教授，变成一个温和偏保守、挺亲资本主义的家伙？我说：是发工资。

turns.en: If you've ever had to make payroll, if you've ever actually had to sell enough of a product of any kind or provide a service of any kind that you are paid for, knowing that you have to put that in the bank because other people are going to pay their bills, the people who work for you are going to pay their bills from that, you get real aware of how hard it is to run a business.
turns.zh: 只要你真发过工资，只要你真卖够过某种产品、提供过某种能收到钱的服务，并且知道这些钱要存进银行，因为给你干活的人要靠它交他们自己的账单——你就会真切体会到经营一家企业有多难。

turns.en: And those young people did an incredible thing, made an incredible product, but as it turns out, making an incredible product is not enough.
turns.zh: 那些年轻人做了一件了不起的事，做出了了不起的产品。但事实证明，光有了不起的产品还不够。

turns.en: You actually have to make an incredible product that the market will reward and do it on a sustained basis, and that's much more difficult. Now, I did a lot of self-experimentation for the book.
turns.zh: 你得做出市场愿意买单的了不起的产品，还得持续地做到——这就难得多了。我为这本书做了大量亲身实验。

turns.en: Like, the whole idea that I had about maybe five years in, four years in was okay. I realized I was kind of making a recipe book of all the things Americans had whipped up to try to get ahead, not just become middle class, but like go from where they were to where they dreamed of being.
turns.zh: 大概做到第四、第五年的时候我意识到：我其实是在编一本食谱，收录所有美国人为了出头绞尽脑汁发明的招数——不只是变成中产，而是从他们所在的地方走到他们梦想成为的地方。

turns.en: And so, all right, well, if it's going to be a recipe book, I need to like eat the cooking. So, everything I could find in the past that people did, I would try in the present.
turns.zh: 所以我想，既然是一本食谱，我就得尝尝自己做的菜。过去的人做过的每一件事，我都在今天试一遍。

turns.en: And the only line that was drawn was my wife saying under no circumstances. But everything below that line, I tried, and one of them was angel investing, right?
turns.zh: 唯一的红线是我太太说的'无论如何不行'。红线以下我全试了，其中之一就是天使投资（angel investing），对吧？

turns.en: Because that was obviously a big, a big part of how we, how we imagine the 90s and 2000s is kind of these angels, investors finding these startups, investing in them before anyone else could and making tons of money.
turns.zh: 因为那显然是我们想象90年代、2000年代的重要部分：天使投资人发掘初创公司，赶在所有人之前投钱，然后大赚一笔。

turns.en: And as it turns out, picking the angels is harder than it looks. So, you also tried shorting stocks recommended by Jim Kramer. Can you talk about that experiment and whether it was educational, profitable, or just kind of good for laughs?
turns.zh: 事实证明，挑对天使比看上去难得多。你还试过做空Jim Cramer推荐的股票。能讲讲那个实验吗？它长见识、赚到钱，还是纯粹图一乐？

turns.en: It was all three. Yeah. So, there's an economics paper and I can't remember exactly what year it came out that showed that Jim Kramer showed mad money under a very strict set of criteria.
turns.zh: 三者兼有。有一篇经济学论文——不记得哪年发表——证明在非常严格的一整套条件下，Jim Cramer的《Mad Money》节目存在可套利的规律。

turns.en: And I need to emphasize that point because I don't want anybody to hear this and just go shorting everything Jim Kramer says. But under a very strict set of criteria, when Jim Kramer on his show mad money would recommend a buy on a stock, you could short that stock because it would bounce for 50 to 55 days and come back to Earth.
turns.zh: 这一点我必须强调，因为我不希望任何人听完就去无差别做空Jim Cramer说的一切。只有在极其严格的一套条件下：当Jim Cramer在《Mad Money》里对某只股票喊出买入时，你可以做空它，因为它会先往上蹿50到55天，然后摔回地面。

turns.en: And in that 50 to 55 days, you could short it. Well, because I was trying everything else I was finding, I decided to try that. And for three months of my life, I sat glued to a television waiting for all of those factors to align, which it occasionally did.
turns.zh: 在那50到55天里你可以做空它。既然我把书里找到的其他东西都在试，我就决定试试这个。整整三个月，我守在电视前等所有条件对齐——还真偶尔对齐过。

turns.en: And then I would rush over to the computer and try to short the stock. Believe it or not, I actually beat the market. Now net of fees, because I had a history professor salary.
turns.zh: 然后我冲到电脑前做空那只股票。信不信由你，我确实跑赢了市场。不过扣掉费用之后没有——因为我拿的是历史教授的薪水——

turns.en: I don't know if anybody's ever told you this, but we don't make a lot of money. History professors get paid in prestige, you know, or all professors really, right?
turns.zh: 不知道有没有人跟你说过，我们挣得不多。历史教授是用声望发工资的——或者说所有教授都差不多，对吧？

turns.en: And so I'm taking my small professor salary money and actually it was coming from my daughter's college money and putting it on this gamble.
turns.zh: 于是我把那点微薄的教授薪水——其实动用的是我女儿的大学教育金——押进了这场赌局。

turns.en: And what I learned in that is I actually did beat the market. Net of fees I lost. But while Kramer was yelling at me like I was a child and setting off alarm sirens that were bothering my wife and family, I heard my wife holler for the downstairs, come quick, she's doing it.
turns.zh: 我从中学到的是：我确实跑赢了市场，但扣掉费用是亏的。而且，当Cramer像训小孩一样冲我咆哮、警报铃声吵得我太太和家人不得安宁的时候，我听到太太在楼下喊：快下来！她在走路了！

turns.en: And I missed my daughter's first steps. So I beat the market. Was it worth it? And the point that I try to make in the book, but it being educational, is actually there's all this rhetoric around you can't beat the market, so don't try.
turns.zh: 我错过了女儿迈出人生第一步。跑赢了市场，值吗？我在书里想说的——除了确实长见识之外——是：围绕'你跑不赢市场，所以别试'的那一整套修辞——

turns.en: I actually find that literature to be pretty paper thin. I know there's a lot of those studies. What they're actually measuring is professional money managers ability to beat the market, which is a very different thing than saying you can't, because professional money managers are operating in a very constrained environment.
turns.zh: 我觉得那些文献其实薄得像纸。我知道有很多那样的研究，但它们度量的其实是职业基金经理跑赢市场的能力，这和说'你做不到'完全是两码事，因为职业基金经理是在非常受限的环境下运作的。

turns.en: And bluntly, if you can't beat the market, then Warren Buffett doesn't exist. You actually, there's another study that shows that certain money managers, especially managing $600 billion more, do tend to beat the market by about one half of 1%.
turns.zh: 坦白说，如果市场不可能跑赢，那Warren Buffett就不存在。其实还有另一项研究显示，某些基金经理——尤其管理着6000亿美元以上资金的那些——确实倾向于跑赢市场大约0.5%。

turns.en: Which if you multiply that by $600 billion is a ton of money. But if you take the average 401k balance and you tried to do what that money manager does, which by the way you can't, but let's just imagine, which is you got to go to Yale for four years and pay tuition.
turns.zh: 那乘以6000亿美元，是一大笔钱。但你要是拿一个普通401k的平均余额去模仿那位基金经理的做法——顺便说你模仿不了，就当能——那意味着你得先去Yale念四年、交学费，

turns.en: You got to work a grueling internship. And then you need to work 70 to 80 hour work weeks. You would eke out an additional $500 a year for the average American's 401k balance.
turns.zh: 再熬过一段辛苦到爆的实习，然后每周工作七八十个小时。最后你能为普通美国人的401k余额一年多抠出500美元。

turns.en: Not the gains that you make. The extra 500 is what you get for all the 80 hour work weeks. Well, that's one night in a hotel in Miami in hurricane season.
turns.zh: 那不是投资收益，那多出来的500美元是你用所有80小时工作周换来的。这就相当于飓风季在Miami住一晚酒店。

turns.en: It's not worth it. And so I try to tell people, can you beat the market? Sure. Do you want to? Probably not. Probably want to use the market to beat your own personal goals.
turns.zh: 不值得。所以我会告诉大家：能跑赢市场吗？能。想跑赢吗？大概不想。你更该用市场去跑赢你自己的人生目标。

turns.en: And that's good enough for most people. Another interesting point in the book is that stocks haven't always been good long-term investments.
turns.zh: 对大多数人来说，这就够了。书里另一个有意思的点是：股票并不总是好的长期投资。

turns.en: And if you look at history up until about 1862, there were some extended periods when stocks actually had negative returns and bonds outperformed.
turns.zh: 如果你往前看历史，直到大约1862年，都还存在一些很长的时段，股票的回报实际是负的，债券反而跑赢。

turns.en: Why is that part of market history largely ignored? Yeah. So I think it's largely ignored because it's not a very good story. So we have a story that we want to be true.
turns.zh: 为什么这段市场历史基本被忽略？是。我想被忽略是因为它不是个好故事。我们心里有一个希望成真的故事，

turns.en: So that's the story we tell. And Jeremy Segal came out with his book, you know, Stocks for the Long Run. And that was a story everyone wanted to hear.
turns.zh: 所以我们就讲那个故事。Jeremy Siegel出了那本《Stocks for the Long Run》，那是人人都想听的故事。

turns.en: And look, I'm not trying to throw shade on Segal's book at all. But the reality is it was a very good book for the data set he used, but the data set he used was not complete.
turns.zh: 我不是要贬低Siegel的书。但现实是，就他所用的数据集而言那是本好书，可他的数据集并不完整。

turns.en: Why was it not complete? Because it's actually really hard to know what all the stocks and the returns were for all of American history. Let's start with the fact that Wall Street wasn't the Wall Street we think of today.
turns.zh: 为什么不完整？因为要弄清美国全部历史里所有股票及其回报，其实非常难。先说一点：Wall Street从来不是我们今天以为的那个Wall Street。

turns.en: There were probably a dozen plus stock markets that were actively trading stocks and not all the stocks in one traded on all the others. There was a stock market in Connecticut.
turns.zh: 当时活跃交易的股票交易所恐怕有十几家不止，而且一家挂牌的股票并不在别家都能交易。Connecticut有自己的证交所，

turns.en: Obviously it was one Chestnut Street in Philadelphia. There's one in South Carolina. One of the most active was Nantes, Mississippi. But no one goes back and looks at the Nantes, Mississippi stock market to see what the returns were because in the long run they were pretty abysmal.
turns.zh: Philadelphia在Chestnut Street上也有一家，South Carolina也有一家。最活跃的之一在密西西比州的Natchez。但没人回头去查Natchez证交所的回报，因为长期看惨不忍睹。

turns.en: So when you actually piece together all the stocks you could buy for all of American history, it turns out bonds beat stocks for most of the 1800s.
turns.zh: 所以当你真正拼出美国历史上所有买得到的股票，会发现整个十九世纪大部分时间，债券跑赢股票。

turns.en: They were tied until about World War II and stocks have been beating bonds ever since, except for a few 15 plus year periods when a few moments when bonds outperformed.
turns.zh: 两者打平，大约到二战前后；此后股票一直在赢债券，除了几个超过15年的时段里债券曾阶段性反超。

turns.en: What does that mean? It means that stocks for the long run is true, but only as old as our last two presidents. And that is not a universal law of history.
turns.zh: 这意味着什么？意味着'股票长期跑赢'是真的，但这个'长期'只有我们最近两任总统那么久。这不是一条普世的历史定律。

turns.en: I'm a historian. In my line of work we call that a rounding error. So 80 years is a lot of time, but it's not enough time to know exactly how things will always work going forward.
turns.zh: 我是历史学家，在我们这行那叫舍入误差。80年是很长时间，但不足以让你确定以后永远会这么走。

turns.en: Now I'm not trying to say invest in bonds over stocks. That's not what I'm saying. I'm just pointing out people have an illusion of history that is an illusion.
turns.zh: 我不是说该买债券不买股票，不是那个意思。我只是指出，人们怀抱的那种历史感是一种幻觉。

turns.en: And we would do better just be frank about the fact that every historical era is different. What worked in different historical eras was different.
turns.zh: 我们不如坦率承认：每个历史时代都不一样，各个时代管用的东西也不一样。

turns.en: So let's not try to learn the lessons of 1850 as if that's a stock market strategy we can employ today, because they lived in a very different world than you live in.
turns.zh: 所以别把1850年的教训当成今天能用的股市策略，因为他们生活的世界和你生活的世界天差地别。

turns.en: One of your strongest findings is that marriage has historically been one of the best predictors of financial success. So can you talk about how you arrived at that and what characteristics make for a financially successful marriage?
turns.zh: 你最强的发现之一是：婚姻在历史上是财务成功最好的预测指标之一。能讲讲你是怎么得出这个结论的吗？什么样的婚姻在财务上更容易成功？

turns.en: Great question. I arrived at that because you couldn't avoid it when you looked. Like if you actually look at the financial advice people were receiving for most of history, a lot of it was intertwined as marriage advice.
turns.zh: 好问题。得出这个结论，是因为你只要去看就绕不开它。历史上人们收到的理财建议，很多都和婚姻建议交织在一起。

turns.en: This is true for men and women, by the way. And I actually think this holds all the way to the present day. In fact, there's some wonderful, oh, and the book title just escaped me, so I will be kicking myself that I can't remember the title.
turns.zh: 顺便说，这对男女都成立。而且我认为这个规律一直延续到今天。事实上有一本特别好的书……唉，书名到嘴边又忘了，回头我得捶自己。

turns.en: There's this wonderful book that looks at some of the modern billionaires, the lesser known billionaires, the really successful Wall Street investors, and kind of ask them about their life and says, what's the through line?
turns.zh: 那本书研究了现代亿万富翁里一批不那么出名的人——真正成功的Wall Street投资人——去问他们的人生，问贯穿其中的那条线是什么。

turns.en: Like what are the real lessons you take away? And almost every one of them says they're spouse. There's like spouse to this day is a strong indicator of financial success.
turns.zh: 真正带得走的经验教训是什么？几乎每个人说的都是自己的配偶。时至今日，配偶依然是财务成功的强指标。

turns.en: So if you go to the history books, it's everywhere. People are talking about the financial wisdom of the right kind of marriage. If you go to the 1840s, there's this card game.
turns.zh: 翻开历史书，这种说法到处都是。人们在讲'好婚姻是理财上的聪明'。回到1840年代，有一款纸牌游戏。

turns.en: I don't know if I have kids and one of the things that's a great joy of parenting is forcing your kids to play a game they don't want to play because you as a parent have something you want to teach them.
turns.zh: 不知道你们有没有孩子，但为人父母的一大乐趣，就是逼孩子玩一个他们并不想玩的游戏，因为当父母的有东西想借游戏教给他们。

turns.en: There's this card game in the 1840s where you would play as a family at night and you're trying to draw the cards that will give the winner is the person who has the best spouse and you're drawing characteristics of a spouse as you go.
turns.zh: 1840年代那款纸牌游戏，一家人晚上围着玩，规则是：赢家是抽到'最好配偶'的人，你一张一张抽配偶的特质卡。

turns.en: And parents are making their kids play this game because they're trying to teach them like maybe the bad breath card is not so bad but also we're holding the work ethic card.
turns.zh: 父母逼孩子玩这个，是在教他们：口臭那张牌也许没那么糟，但我们手里攥着的是'勤劳肯干'这张牌。

turns.en: So it was so important to parents to teach young people this. If you go into the novels of the late 1800s, there's a whole genre of novels in which young women are having to make decisions about some rapacious man who's after her in some way, usually tied to money and inheritance.
turns.zh: 对父母来说，教会年轻人这件事太重要了。再到十九世纪末的小说里，有一整个类型，讲的都是年轻女性要面对某个贪婪男人的图谋，往往和钱、继承权纠缠不清。

turns.en: And you know how Zach Gallifanakis is kind of the universal sidekick in our movies today or Shrek's Tonki. Like there's always this sidekick character who's always an Aria male.
turns.zh: 你知道，就像今天电影里Zach Galifianakis是那种万金油跟班，或者《Shrek》里的驴子——总有这样一个配角，而且总归是个男性。

turns.en: In their era it was a female. It was the female best friend of the woman who was the center of the novel. And her best friend always ends up marrying just for love and not thinking about the financial issues and she always ends up in a terrible situation.
turns.zh: 在她们那个年代，这个角色是女性：是小说女主角身边那位闺蜜。而这位闺蜜总是只为爱情嫁人、从不考虑财务问题，结局总是凄惨。

turns.en: Like that was the kind of running joke of novels of that period. So not thinking about the finances of your marriage could get you and that's what people wanted you to understand.
turns.zh: 那几乎是那个年代小说的保留笑点。所以，不替你婚姻的财务着想是会害了你的——那就是人们想让你明白的事。

turns.en: Now it did not just mean marrying up and into more money. It meant marrying into the kind of person who you could build something with of the course of your lifetime.
turns.zh: 这并不只是'往上嫁、嫁进更多钱'。而是嫁一个你终其一生可以与之共同建设点什么的人。

turns.en: Because at the end of the day, you're two people sitting over the kitchen table with a yellow legal pad running a small nonprofit. And you have to figure out how you're going to manage this.
turns.zh: 因为到头来，就是两个人坐在厨房桌边，就着一张黄色便签本，经营一个小小的非营利机构，你们得自己想办法把一切运转起来。

turns.en: By the way, this still holds today. To this day, marriage is one of the strongest predictors. The quality of a marriage is one of the strongest predictors of financial outcomes that we have.
turns.zh: 顺便说，这个到今天依然成立。时至今日，婚姻质量依然是我们已知的、对财务结果最强的预测指标之一。

turns.en: And it confounds things you would not expect it to confound. Married black men earn more than single white men. Married women at the age of 55 are earning 2x what single women at the age of 55 are earning.
turns.zh: 它在很多你意想不到的维度上成立：已婚黑人男性的收入高于单身白人男性；55岁的已婚女性收入是55岁单身女性的2倍。

turns.en: Married men's net worth at retirement wildly outperform single men's net worth at retirement. Same sex married couples out earn heterosexuals who are single of their same age cohort.
turns.zh: 已婚男性退休时的净资产大幅优于单身男性；同性已婚家庭的收入高于同龄的单身异性恋。

turns.en: Like it just confounds everything you would think it wouldn't confound. So there's just something about marriage that you don't choose the family you start with.
turns.zh: 它在一切你以为它不会起作用的维度上都起作用。婚姻之所以特别，是因为你没法选择你出身的那个家庭。

turns.en: So the family you end up starting is one of the biggest things under your control. And as it turns out, marriage is a superpower because capitalism is a team sport.
turns.zh: 而你自己最终建立的那个家庭，恰恰是你最能掌控的大事之一。事实证明，婚姻是一种超能力，因为资本主义是团队运动。

turns.en: And you just win more games playing on two player mode. And this kind of makes sense when you think about it. Like there's risks that each of you can take that you can only take because the other one is there to cover the risks.
turns.zh: 双人模式就是会赢更多局。这道理一想就通：你们各自敢去冒的那些险，正因为有另一个人兜底才敢去冒。

turns.en: Right. There's like you stay late at night. I'll take the kids to check. They may they may eat Chick-fil-A. Right. Like it may not have told my wife many times like they may not eat what you would want them to eat.
turns.zh: 比如你晚上留下来加班，我去接孩子、管晚饭，他们也许吃的是Chick-fil-A。我常跟太太说，他们吃的也许不是你希望他们吃的，

turns.en: But you stay late and do what you need to do to advance your career. And I'll handle this. If you compound that over the lifetime of a career, there's promotions in there you don't otherwise get.
turns.zh: 但你留下来，把推进事业该做的事做完，家里我来搞定。把这个因素复利到你整个职业生涯里，就意味着那些本来轮不到你的晋升。

turns.en: And you could just see this over and over and over for men and for women. Marriage is one of the biggest predictors of financial success. Another adventure you had was investing in real estate, owning and renting out homes.
turns.zh: 这在男人身上、女人身上都能反复看到。婚姻是财务成功最大的预测指标之一。你还有另一段冒险：投资房地产，持有并出租房屋。

turns.en: And you as a landlord had to deal with hoarders, human traffickers, squatters, the FBI. Does the real estate industry kind of undersell how difficult owning real estate and being a landlord really is?
turns.zh: 你当房东，跟囤积症住户、人贩子、占屋者，还有FBI都打过交道。房地产行业是不是把持有房产和当房东的实际难度给轻描淡写了？

turns.en: Oh, of course, because otherwise who would show up to the seminars? My book is not an advertisement for real estate investing, although it worked out well for me.
turns.zh: 那是当然，不然谁会来听讲座。我那本书不是房地产投资的广告——尽管它对我来说效果不错。

turns.en: So one of the many things I mean, I tried so many self experiments in this book. I Airbnb'd all the rooms in my house because believe it or not, that was how Americans paid off their mortgage.
turns.zh: 我在这本书里做了太多自我实验：我把家里所有房间都挂上Airbnb出租，因为信不信由你，那曾经是美国人还清按揭的方式。

turns.en: That was the primary financial advice about how to pay off your mortgage early was to rent out rooms in your house for a long, long time. One in three Americans at any given time was a landlord for most of history because they were trying to pay off their house.
turns.zh: 怎么提前还清按揭——长久以来最主要的理财建议就是把自己家的房间租出去。历史上任何时刻，三个美国人里就有一个当过房东，就为了还清自己的房子。

turns.en: I, you know, all kinds of crazy stuff. I bought land on the moon because that was a big rage in the early space era of people like trying to claim they own the moon.
turns.zh: 我干过各种疯狂事。我买过月球上的地，因为太空时代早期刮那阵流行风，人们抢着声称自己拥有月球。

turns.en: But one of the things that comes out of World War II is you get a housing shortage and housing shortages, believe it or not, it's hard to believe today especially, but believe it or not, housing shortages were pretty rare in American history because you could build it pretty fast.
turns.zh: 但二战带来的一件事是房荒。住房短缺——尤其今天听起来难以置信，但信不信由你——在美国历史上其实相当罕见，因为房子可以盖得很快。

turns.en: But coming out of World War II, there was a housing shortage and because of that, people who had housing, especially rental properties, did really well.
turns.zh: 可二战结束后真的出现了住房短缺，于是有房的人——尤其是持有出租物业的人——赚得极好。

turns.en: And so then the first one of these to write a book about it in the 1950s, called How I Became a Millionaire in My Spare Time, becomes a bestseller.
turns.zh: 1950年代，第一个靠这个写书的人——书名《How I Became a Millionaire in My Spare Time》——成了畅销书。

turns.en: And people start teaching courses on real estate investing, how to get into it. That's a pretty low inflationary environment in the 50s and 60s, but then in the late 60s and 70s, inflation just explodes upwards and so does real estate investing.
turns.zh: 于是人们开始开班教房地产投资、教你怎么进场。五六十年代通胀环境相当低，但到六十年代末和七十年代，通胀一飞冲天，房地产投资也跟着起飞。

turns.en: And so people are rushing to try to buy a house with as little money down as possible and to teach other people how to do it. And by doing that, the logic is, well, if the house is going to go up by 10% just because of inflation and you put down very little, you get the entire gain on that house and the return on your actual invested capital is huge.
turns.zh: 大家抢着付尽可能少的首付买房，再教别人怎么买。逻辑是：只要通胀把房价推高10%，而你首付极低，你就吃下这套房的全部涨幅，实际投入资本的回报率大得惊人。

turns.en: And there's this race to the bottom on this that becomes almost, not almost, it becomes darkly humorous so that by the early 1980s, there's actually a book that sold pretty well that told people to not only buy a house with no money down, buy it when you actually have no money in your checking account.
turns.zh: 于是形成了逐底竞争，到后来——不是'近乎'黑色幽默，就是黑色幽默：1980年代初真有一本卖得不错的书，教人们不但零首付买房，而且是在你支票账户里真一分钱都没有的情况下去买。

turns.en: But as long as you can take the, at the closing table, they'll hand you the security deposits for the renters, the tenants, and you can rush to the bank.
turns.zh: 只要你办交割的时候，他们把租客们的押金交到你手上，你就能冲向银行——

turns.en: This is the 80s, you're not doing this on your phone. You could rush to the bank and deposit it before your check clears and then you basically kited the check, put the money in.
turns.zh: 那可是八十年代，没法用手机操作。你得赶在自己的支票兑付之前跑到银行把钱存进去，说白了就是吃空头支票的时间差（check kiting），把钱填进去。

turns.en: It's by the way illegal, can't do that. It was illegal then, it's illegal now. Well anyway, in this idea of like I'm going to try out everything they tried then, I decided I would try little money down real estate investing, again to try to show people what is it like to try to do what they did now.
turns.zh: 顺便说这是违法的，千万别干。那时候违法，现在也违法。无论如何，本着'当年他们试过的我都要试'的念头，我决定试试低首付房地产投资，也是想让大家看看，今天照搬当年那套是什么滋味。

turns.en: And I tried this of course in the post-2008 crash, so in the early 20s, going around in real estate investing, if you look at it back today, people are like, well duh, of course you made money.
turns.zh: 我当然是在2008年崩盘之后试的，也就是二十年代初。现在回头看，大家会说：那还用问，你当然赚到钱了。

turns.en: I promise you it was not as easy as it sounded. You could find houses for really cheap. You couldn't find people to lend you the money, and the people living in those houses, especially working class houses, were, you know, were people who had their own issues that they were dealing with.
turns.zh: 我向你保证，没有听起来那么容易。超便宜的房子你找得到，但借你钱的人你找不到。而住在那类房子里的人——尤其工薪阶层的房子——都有各自要面对的难处。

turns.en: And I went out to buy a house, went looking in a corridor outside of Charlotte, North Carolina, and I ended up buying a house and a four-unit apartment building.
turns.zh: 我出门买房，在North Carolina的Charlotte外围一条走廊一带找，结果我买了一栋房子，还有一栋四户公寓楼。

turns.en: And I came home, my wife was like, I said you could buy one. I was like, well, it was a good deal. You know, like, I don't know, they talked me into it.
turns.zh: 回到家，我太太说：'我说过你可以买一栋来着。'我说：'可是真划算啊。我也不知道，反正被他们说动了。'

turns.en: And we renovated the house, and a woman came out of the woodwork and said I'd love to rent it. I already own a home, I just have to move for work for a few years.
turns.zh: 我们翻新完房子，一位女士冒出来想租。她说自己本来有房，只是因为工作需要搬过去几年。

turns.en: I was like, oh, this is great, and we never saw her again. And it turns out she worked for a temp agency that was managing the lithium mines of North Carolina where they were importing illegal labor.
turns.zh: 我心想太好了，然后就再也没见过她。结果她在一家劳务中介工作，而那家中介在给North Carolina的锂矿引进非法劳工。

turns.en: And so before I knew it, 40-something Haitian immigrants were living in my one-three bedroom house. And I went to the cops who went to the FBI, and they said, look, this is a human trafficking ring.
turns.zh: 等我反应过来，我那三居室里住了四十多个海地移民。我去找警察，警察转手找了FBI，他们说：这是一个人口贩运团伙。

turns.en: You can evict them if you want, but we'd really appreciate if you'd let us sit on it so we could stake it out and kind of track it. And I grit my teeth, and so that sounds like what I should do.
turns.zh: 你想驱逐可以，但我们特别希望你先按兵不动，好让我们蹲守、追踪。我咬咬牙——听上去确实该这么做。

turns.en: And before I know it, like, I'm on a conference call at the FBI, and they're like raiding my rental property. By the way, all of those renovations were destroyed because you just can't have 40 people living in a house of three bedrooms.
turns.zh: 再等我回过神来，我已经和FBI开上电话会，他们要去查抄我的出租屋了。顺便说，所有装修全毁了——三居室的房子里塞四十个人是根本不行的。

turns.en: But in the part that building, I had hoarders, which then that we had rats, which meant that the rats from the hoarders were getting into the other apartments.
turns.zh: 而那栋公寓楼里，我碰上过囤积症住户，然后是老鼠——囤积户那里的老鼠窜进了其他公寓。

turns.en: And I had to go and I politely informed them, you can't do that here, right? Like, your neighbors are suffering because of what you're doing.
turns.zh: 我只好上门，客气地告诉他们：不能这么干。你的邻居正在为你的所作所为遭殃。

turns.en: And they probably pulled a shotgun on me. And I distinctly remember leaping off the steps, trying to run to my car with a shotgun pointed at my back.
turns.zh: 对方差点掏出猎枪指着我。我清楚地记得自己从台阶上跳下去就往车里跑，背后是一支猎枪——

turns.en: That had just a second ago been pointed at my belly. And instead of thinking about my life and my children, all I could remember was this old rock song, Give Me Three Steps, Give Me Three Steps, Mr.
turns.zh: 那支枪前一秒还抵着我的肚子。那一刻我满脑子想的不是自己和孩子的安危，而是那首老摇滚：Give Me Three Steps, Give Me Three Steps, Mr.

turns.en: And I'm just running for dear life thinking about this old rock song my dad used to listen to. And as I'm driving away, I finally thought, I may have made a mistake.
turns.zh: 我玩命狂奔，脑子里回响的是我爸从前常听的这首老歌。等我开车驶离，才终于想到：我可能犯了个大错。

turns.en: This might not be for me. But I sat down and I thought, well, this is probably as bad as real estate investing can get. So what if I run this like a business and see how, you know, what's the upside?
turns.zh: 这行也许不适合我。但我坐下来想：房地产投资大概坏也坏不到哪儿去了。那我要是把它当一门生意来经营，看看上限在哪？

turns.en: And so over time, I just got really good at it. It helped that I was raised by a dad who was an electrician. And so far I knew that what I owned was not homes, but what I owned was, you know, two by fours and electrical wire and pipes.
turns.zh: 于是时间一长，我竟真做成了。有个电工出身的爹帮了大忙。我早就明白：我拥有的不是'房子'，而是一根根2x4木方、电线和水管。

turns.en: And so I kind of understood intuitively what to do when things went wrong. But also I just kind of decided to eat my own cooking. What was the one lesson of history to get ahead?
turns.zh: 所以出了毛病，我凭直觉就知道该怎么办。而且我也决定吃自己做的菜。关于出人头地，历史的头号教训是什么？

turns.en: Concentration and then diversify. You diversify at the end of your life down at the beginning. And so I decided I'm going to go all in. I'm going to concentrate and see if I can make a million dollars.
turns.zh: 先集中，后分散。分散是你人生尾声该做的事，开头要集中。于是我决定全情投入、押注集中，看自己能不能赚到一百万美元。

turns.en: And to my great surprise, I overshot and one day looked up and I was like, honey, I think we're millionaires. And then it kept going and kept going.
turns.zh: 令我非常意外的是，我还超额完成了。有一天我抬起头说：亲爱的，我觉得我们成百万富翁了。然后它一路涨、一路涨。

turns.en: And eventually I was able to just say, all right, I can just sit at home and write. And that was a, it was an interesting experience. So I have failed upwards as an academic into a place where I never thought I'd be.
turns.zh: 最终我可以干脆坐在家中写作。那是一段奇妙的经历。作为一个学者，我'向上失败'，走到了一个自己从没敢想的位置。

turns.en: Well, Amy and I have a million more questions for you, but I'm curious to find out how you see your career evolve going forward. Do you view yourself primarily as an academic, a journalist and writer, real estate investor?
turns.zh: Amy和我还有一百万个问题想问你，但我很好奇你会怎么看自己事业未来的走向。你主要把自己看作学者、记者兼作家，还是房地产投资人？

turns.en: What do you think you'll be doing in the future? Well, thank you for having the time to have this conversation. I think going forward, I am at some level who I've always been, which is a kid from the rural South who fell in love with history and wanted to teach other people about it.
turns.zh: 你觉得未来自己会做什么？谢谢你抽出时间完成这次对话。我想，往前走，我在某个层面上还是原来那个人：一个来自南方农村、爱上历史、想把历史讲给别人听的孩子。

turns.en: And so I really think of myself, everything I'm doing is in some degree trying to educate and inspire people to get excited about something.
turns.zh: 所以我对自己的定位是：我做的每一件事，某种程度上都是在教育和激励人们，让他们对某件事兴奋起来。

turns.en: Because I promise you, if you teach the 8 a.m. U.S. History Survey for five years of your life, you have to figure out how to make history really exciting to those kids who do not want to be there in this slot.
turns.zh: 我向你保证，如果你教过五年早上8点的美国历史通识课，你就必须学会怎么让历史真正带劲——对那些根本不想在这个时段待在教室里的孩子。

turns.en: Most of whom are the football team because they have practice this afternoon. And so I really, that's kind of what I do with my life is I'm trying to make history fun, exciting, enjoyable, but also useful.
turns.zh: 那教室里多半是橄榄球队的，因为下午要训练。所以，我这辈子做的事，就是让历史变得有趣、带劲、享受，而且有用。

turns.en: And whether I'm writing on my sub-stack, which I try to do like once a month an essay on how history can teach you about finances and markets and these kinds of things.
turns.zh: 不管是在我的Substack上写文章——我尽量每月一篇，讲历史怎么教你看懂财务和市场——

turns.en: Or whether it's giving, you know, I go around, I give talks, you know, presentations, writing other books in the future. I do love being a writer. Writing is one of my great passions.
turns.zh: 还是到处去做演讲、做分享、将来写别的书。我确实热爱作家的身份，写作是我最大的热情之一。

turns.en: But at the end of the day, it's all kind of bundled together by the desire to make all of this fun, interesting and useful. So whether that's writing it down or speaking it, that's it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 但归根结底，把它们捆在一起的是同一个愿望：让这一切有趣、有料、有用。所以是写下来还是讲出来，都一样。是的。

turns.zh: 是啊。Joseph，非常感谢你来参加节目，我们真的聊得很开心。我也非常享受这次对话，太谢谢你们了。

turns.en: And I look forward to more conversations in the future. Really appreciate it. Thanks so much, Joseph. Thank you for joining us on the Long View.
turns.zh: 我也期待未来有更多对话，真的非常感激。多谢你，Joseph。谢谢你来The Long View。
